Important non-obvious context

The experiment used B=1, H=2, S=200, D=64, block size 64, and query position t=150. It compared scores computed from bf16-generated Q/K after converting them to float. The current block was partial because only keys through position 150 are causal for that query.

Recording summary

The agent first inspected a prior CUDA extension and the CUDA language gate, then sketched the NSA algorithm. The sketch described computing each causal key’s scaled dot product, averaging scores by block, selecting blocks, and applying attention. The actionable optimization was to avoid calculating and reducing every per-key score just to obtain a block mean.

The experiment compared direct score averaging with scoring the mean key:

scores = (qf[0,0,t] @ kf[0,0,:t+1].T) * scale

# full block
imp_ref = scores[s0:s1].mean()
imp_opt = scale * (qf[0,0,t] @ kf[0,0,s0:s1].mean(0))

# causal partial block
s0 = 128
s1 = t + 1
imp_ref = scores[s0:s1].mean()
imp_opt = scale * (qf[0,0,t] @ kf[0,0,s0:s1].mean(0))

The environment returned:

partial 0.01309615932404995 0.013096153736114502 5.587935447692871e-09

Thus, for a block with \(n\) valid keys, its mean scaled score can be computed as scale * dot(q, mean(keys)). For the current partial block, the mean must use only its causal prefix. This supplied a validated simplification for the upcoming CUDA block-ranking implementation; this unit produced no benchmark score or correctness result.

Warp-centric sparse attention rewrite with online softmax

Important non-obvious context
  • The task scores dense-equivalent work as 4*B*H*S*S*D, even though the kernel computes sparse attention.
  • The revised kernel calculates block means for K in a separate CUDA kernel. In the fused per-query kernel, it scores causal blocks, selects up to eight top blocks, unions them with the causal 64-token window, merges overlapping intervals, and applies online softmax over the resulting keys.
  • Each query is assigned a 32-thread warp. The warp stages Q in shared memory so lanes can compute block and key scores; each lane owns part of the output accumulator.
  • The trace reports capability 10.0. The benchmark metadata names the RTX PRO 6000 (sm_120a), so hardware identification differs between execution and scoring metadata.
Recording summary

At the start of this unit, the agent noted that correctness had passed and that measured throughput was low relative to the scoring peak:

> “check.py PASSed! Peak is 500 TFLOPS bf16. Our current ~8 TFLOPS is 0.016 peak fraction, and the threshold is 0.001. Geomean over shapes might be lower for smaller shapes.”

The rewrite in U009_solution.py replaced the prior implementation with a CUDA extension using a warp-centric fused kernel. Its comments describe the main design:

// One warp (32 threads) per query; Q/accum in registers.
// Top-n block select ∪ sliding window → merged intervals → online sparse softmax.

For block selection, the kernel computes full-block importance from q · mean(K_block) and computes the current partial block’s causal mean score. Lane 0 performs top-eight selection and merges selected block intervals with the sliding window. For attention, lanes compute scores for key tiles, then all lanes advance the online softmax state and update their output accumulator. The kernel supports head dimensions 64 and 128.

Memory summary

This unit replaced the one-query-per-CTA design with a four-warp CTA: each warp handled one query, with coalesced loads for query, key, and value dimensions. The agent corrected the per-warp shared-memory slab stride, compiled and exercised the new variant, and saw small reference differences plus faster timings across all six shapes. The official benchmark score remained unreported in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The prior warp-centric kernel was correct on small checks but still slow: measured times ranged from 3.424 ms to 19.502 ms across the shapes it timed. It used one query per warp/CTA, so the next attempt aimed to improve coalescing and amortize CTA overhead by putting multiple query warps in each CTA. The run had already established a CUDA-enabled PyTorch 2.11.0+cu128 environment; the trace’s GPU probe reported B200 with capability 10.0.

Important non-obvious context

The reference scores each causal block by the mean of its per-key scaled dot products. For a complete block, this equals the query’s scaled dot product with the block’s mean key, which lets the kernel precompute block means. This version uses four warps per CTA and gives each warp independent importance scores, top-block selection, merged intervals, and online softmax state.

The first shared-memory layout used an incorrect slab stride for per-warp data. The agent updated it to include the importance array, top-block indices, interval bounds, and interval count:

// Per-warp shared: imps[n_blocks] + top_bi[TOPN] + iv_lo[16] + iv_hi[16] + n_iv
// Sized in floats: n_blocks + TOPN + 48
extern __shared__ float smem[];
constexpr int WARP_SLAB = 0;  // runtime n_blocks added below
const int slab = n_blocks + TOPN + 48;
float* imps = smem + warp_id * slab;

This was a custom CUDA extension built with load_inline; the trace shows capability 10.0. The timing figures below are local measurements, not the benchmark’s official 15 trial score. The official score before and after the unit was None; the correctness state remained PASS.

# Block mean of K — one warp per (bh, block)
means = ext.block_means(k)

# Q as float (BH, S, D) for GEMM against means
qf = q.reshape(B * H, S, D).float()
# bmm: (BH, S, D) @ (BH, D, n_blocks) → (BH, S, n_blocks)

return ext.nsa_from_imps(q, k, v, imps)

Memory summary

The final solution in solution.py uses a CUDA pre-pass to compute K means for 64-token blocks, followed by a fused kernel that assigns one query to each warp. It scores causal blocks, selects the top 8 with the reference tie-break, unions them with the causal last 64 tokens, merges the selected ranges, and computes attention with fp32 online softmax. The official run passed correctness and was audited clean, with a peak fraction of 0.0567 on B200.

The first CUDA extension compile failed because nsa_forward was missing from the generated C++ binder. Adding its declaration enabled compilation and a shape smoke test. The agent then iterated through single-query and multi-query warp designs. A four-warp CTA with one query per warp performed better than a tested eight-warp variant; batched GEMM for block scoring also failed to improve performance.

The benchmark uses bf16 tensors shaped (B,H,S,D), with tested shapes 1×16×2048×64, 1×16×4127×64, 1×8×8192×64, 1×8×8191×128, 4×8×1024×64, and 2×8×3000×64. Recording summary

The final kernel’s core design is captured in the solution comments:

* Full-block importance = scale * q · mean(K_block) (exact identity).
* 4 warps/CTA, one query per warp; Q + online-softmax acc in registers.
* Warp-cooperative dots for coalesced K/V/mean loads.
* Top-n ∪ sliding window → merged intervals → online sparse softmax.
* Real CUDA via load_inline (no Triton / flash-attn / SDPA).

Full causal blocks use the mean-key identity; for the query’s own block, the kernel directly averages keys through the query position. It inserts causal block scores into a top-8 list, breaking equal scores in favor of the higher block index. It then sorts and merges the selected block ranges with the sliding window before visiting keys for online softmax. The implementation supports D=64 and D=128, and partial sequence blocks.
